newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India can become largest rice producer.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India can become largest rice producer.

text.p: India can displace China as the world's biggest rice producer if irrigation is extended to cover more farmland, an international rice expert said.

"India has the capacity to double the yields under rain-fed areas by bringing more area under irrigated cultivation," George Rothschild, director general of the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), told Reuters in an interview at the weekend.
"If it could achieve that, I have no doubt that India would become the number one (rice) producer in the world."
Rothschild said India has nearly 48 million hectares (120 million acres) of land under rice cultivation, but only 18 million hectares (45 million acres) are irrigated.
China, currently the largest producer, harvests all its rice from irrigated lands and has achieved its productivity potential, he said.
Rothschild said rice cropland in eastern India was yielding far less than it could for lack of water.
"Areas under rice cultivation in eastern India are currently yielding only 1.75 to two tonnes of rice per hectare. Yields can be increased (to) up to four tonnes," Rothschild said.
Eastern India currently has 50 percent of the total area under rice cultivation but accounts for only 35 percent of the country's rice output.
Rothschild said India's rice production over the past few years had grown steadily.
"Looking at the productivity gains which are bieng achieved, I think that India could lift its exports by another 20 to 30 percent annually," he said.
He said Indian exports were expected to pick up because in other rice exporting countries such as Thailand, farmers were moving from rice cultivation to other lucrative crops.
India produced nearly 81 million tonnes of rice in the 1995/96 year ended on June 30. It exported a record 5.5 million tonnes of rice, emerging as the largest exporter after Thailand.
A net importer of foodgrains until the 1980s, India has become self-reliant in agriculture since a "green revolution" emphasising increased productivity was launched in the 1960s.
Over the past two years, it has emerged as a net exporter of rice and wheat.
Rothschild said world rice output would be just sufficient to meet international demand, expected to increase by some 70 percent by 2025.
Rothschild said currently the world's annual output was around 560 million tonnes, feeding some 2.3 billion people, 90 percent of whom live in Asia.
By 2025, world rice demand will increase to nearly 800 million tonnes as the number of rice consumers worldwide increases to four billion, he said.
